section.heading: 3.7. Differentials
section.paragraph: The Millers are planning to buy a house in the near future and estimate that they will need a $$30$$ -year fixed-rate mortgage of $$\$ 240,000$$ . If the interest rate increases from the present rate of $$5\%$$ per year to $$5.4\%$$ per year between now and the time the Millers decide to secure the loan, approximately how much more per month will their mortgage be? (You will be asked to answer this question in Exercise 46.)

Questions such as this, in which one wishes to estimate the change in the dependent variable (monthly mortgage payment) corresponding to a small change in the independent variable (interest rate per year), occur in many real-life applications. For example:

list.item: An economist would like to know how a small increase in a country’s capital expenditure will affect the country’s gross domestic output.
A sociologist would like to know how a small increase in the amount of capital investment in a housing project will affect the crime rate.
A businesswoman would like to know how raising a product’s unit price by a small amount will affect her profit.
A bacteriologist would like to know how a small increase in the amount of a bactericide will affect a population of bacteria.

section.paragraph: To calculate these changes and estimate their effects, we use the differential of a function, a concept that will be introduced shortly.
section.heading: Increments
section.paragraph: Let $$x$$ denote a variable quantity and suppose $$x$$ changes from $$x_{1}$$ to $$x_{2}$$ . This change in $$x$$ is called the increment in $$\mathbf{x}$$ and is denoted by the symbol $$\Delta x$$ (read “delta $$x$$ ”). Thus,
$$\Delta x = x_{2} - x_{1} {{Final value} - {initial value}}$$

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Find the increment in $$x$$ as $$x$$ changes

list.item: (a) from $$3$$ to $$3.2$$ and

example.heading: Solution

section.paragraph: Observe that $$\Delta x$$ plays the same role that $$h$$ played in Section 2.4.

Now, suppose two quantities, $$x$$ and $$y$$ , are related by an equation $$y = f(x)$$ , where $$f$$ is a function. If $$x$$ changes from $$x$$ to $$x + \Delta x$$ , then the corresponding change in $$y$$ is called the increment in $$y$$ . It is denoted by $$\Delta y$$ and is defined by
$$\Delta y = f\left( x + \Delta x \right) - f(x)$$
(see Figure 21).

Two parallel lines starting from the y axis at marked points y = f (x), above the x axis and y = f (x + Delta x), above y = f (x) run parallel to the x axis. The distance between the two lines is labeled Delta y. At the point where the line y = f (x) cuts the curve a perpendicular is dropped to the x axis meeting it at x. The line y = f (x + Delta x) meets the curve at an unlabeled point and the perpendicular dropped from this point to the x axis meets the x axis at x + Delta x. The distance between the two perpendiculars is labeled Delta x.

figure.caption: An increment of $$\Delta x$$ in $$x$$ induces an increment of $$\Delta y = f\left( x + \Delta x \right) - f(x)$$ in $$y$$ .

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Let $$y = x^{3}$$ . Find $$\Delta x$$ and $$\Delta y$$ when $$x$$ changes

list.item: (a) from $$2$$ to $$2.01$$ and

example.heading: Solution

list.item: Here, $$\Delta x = 2.01 - 2 = 0.01$$ . Next, $$\begin{array}{l} {\Delta y = f\left( x + \Delta x \right) - f(x) = f(2.01) - f(2)} \\ {\phantom{\Delta y} = (2.01)^{3} - 2^{3} = 8.120601 - 8 = 0.120601} \end{array}$$

Here, $$\Delta x = 1.98 - 2 = - 0.02$$ . Next, $$\begin{array}{l} {\Delta y = f\left( x + \Delta x \right) - f(x) = f(1.98) - f(2)} \\ {\phantom{\Delta y} = (1.98)^{3} - 2^{3} = 7.762392 - 8 = - 0.237608} \end{array}$$

section.heading: Differentials
section.paragraph: We can obtain a relatively quick and simple way of approximating $$\Delta y$$ , the change in $$y$$ due to a small change $$\Delta x$$ , by examining the graph of the function $$f$$ shown in Figure 22.

image.alt: Details A curve y = f (x) and a line T are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The curve begins close to the y axis at the bottom left of the first quadrant a short distance above the x axis, extends upward to the right, bulging away from the y axis. The line begins near the x axis at the bottom left of the quadrant and rises upward to the right and touches the curve at a labeled point P. From the mark x on the x axis, a vertical line rises upward and meets the curve at the point P. From the x + Delta x, another vertical line rises upward to meet the curve at an unlabeled point, cutting the line T on the way. From the point where the vertical line cuts the line T, a short line segment is drawn horizontally to the right. The horizontal distance between these two lines is labeled Delta x. From the marks, f (x) and f (x + Delta x), horizontal lines run to the right parallel to the x axis, cutting the curve at P and an unlabeled point respectively. The vertical distance between the two lines is labeled Delta y. The vertical distance between the line at y = f (x) and the short horizontal line segment were the vertical line at x = x + Delta cuts the line T is labeled d y.

figure.caption: If $$\Delta x$$ is small, $$dy$$ is a good approximation of $$\Delta y$$ .

section.paragraph: Observe that near the point of tangency $$P$$ , the tangent line $$T$$ is close to the graph of $$f$$ . Therefore, if $$\Delta x$$ is small, then $$dy$$ is a good approximation of $$\Delta y$$ . We can find an expression for $$dy$$ as follows. Notice that the slope of $$T$$ is given by
$$\frac{dy}{\Delta x} {{Rise} \div {run}}$$
However, the slope of $$T$$ is given by $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ . Therefore, we have
$$\frac{dy}{\Delta x} = f^{\prime}(x)$$
or $$dy = f^{\prime}(x)\Delta x$$ . Thus, we have the approximation
$$\Delta y \approx dy = f^{\prime}(x)\Delta x$$
in terms of the derivative of $$f$$ at $$x$$ . The quantity $$dy$$ is called the differential of $$y$$ .

note.title: The Differential
note.heading: The Differential
note.paragraph: Let $$y = f(x)$$ define a differentiable function of $$x$$ . Then,

list.item: The differential $$\mathbf{dx}$$ of the independent variable $$x$$ is $$dx = \Delta x$$ .
The differential $$\mathbf{dy}$$ of the dependent variable $$y$$ is (12) $$dy = f^{\prime}(x)\Delta x = f^{\prime}(x)dx$$
For the independent variable $$x$$ : There is no difference between $$\Delta x$$ and $$dx$$ —both measure the change in $$x$$ from $$x$$ to $$x + \Delta x$$ .

For the dependent variable $$y$$ : $$\Delta y$$ measures the actual change in $$y$$ as $$x$$ changes from $$x$$ to $$x + \Delta x$$ , whereas $$dy$$ measures the approximate change in $$y$$ corresponding to the same change in $$x$$ .
The differential $$dy$$ depends on both $$x$$ and $$dx$$ , but for fixed $$x$$ , $$dy$$ is a linear function of $$dx$$ .
Find the differential $$dy$$ of $$y$$ .
Use $$dy$$ to approximate $$\Delta y$$ when $$x$$ changes from $$2$$ to $$2.01$$ .
Use $$dy$$ to approximate $$\Delta y$$ when $$x$$ changes from $$2$$ to $$1.98$$ .
Compare the results of part (b) with those of Example 2.
Let $$f(x) = x^{3}$$ . Then, $$dy = f^{\prime}(x)dx = 3x^{2}dx$$
As you can see, both approximations $$0.12$$ and $$- 0.24$$ are quite close to the actual changes $$\Delta y$$ obtained in Example 2: $$0.120601$$ and $$- 0.237608$$ .

section.paragraph: Observe how much easier it is to find an approximation to the exact change in a function with the help of the differential, rather than calculating the exact change in the function itself. In the following examples, we take advantage of this fact.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Approximate the value of $$\sqrt{26.5}$$ using differentials. Verify your result using the $$\boxed{\sqrt{}}$$ key on your calculator.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Since we want to compute the square root of a number, let’s consider the function $$y = f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ . Since $$25$$ is the number nearest $$26.5$$ whose square root is readily recognized, let’s take $$x = 25$$ . We want to know the change in $$y$$ , $$\Delta y$$ , as $$x$$ changes from $$x = 25$$ to $$x = 26.5$$ , an increase of $$\Delta x = 1.5$$ units. Using Equation (12), we find

$$\begin{array}{l} {\Delta y \approx dy = f^{\prime}(x)\Delta x} \\ {\phantom{\Delta y \approx dy} = \left( \left. \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \right|_{x = 25} \right) \cdot (1.5) = \left( \frac{1}{10} \right)(1.5) = 0.15} \end{array}$$
The exact value of $$\sqrt{26.5}$$ , rounded off to five decimal places, is $$5.14782$$ . Thus, the error incurred in the approximation is $$0.00218$$ .

note.heading: Applied Example 5. The Effect of Speed on Vehicular Operating Cost
note.paragraph: The total cost incurred in operating a certain type of truck on a $$500$$ -mile trip, traveling at an average speed of $$v$$ mph, is estimated to be
dollars. Find the approximate change in the total operating cost when the average speed is increased from $$55$$ mph to $$58$$ mph.
note.heading: Solution
note.paragraph: With $$v = 55$$ and $$\Delta v = dv = 3$$ , we find
$$\begin{array}{l} {\Delta C \approx dC = C^{\prime}(v)dv = {\left( 1 - \frac{4500}{v^{2}} \right)|}_{v = 55} \cdot {(3)}} \\ {= \left( 1 - \frac{4500}{3025} \right)(3) \approx - 1.46} \end{array}$$
so the total operating cost is found to decrease by $$\$ 1.46$$ . This might explain why so many independent truckers often exceed the speed limit where it is $$55$$ mph.

note.paragraph: The relationship between the amount of money $$x$$ spent by Cannon Precision Instruments on advertising and Cannon’s total sales $$S(x)$$ is given by the function

note.heading: Solution

that is, an increase of $$\$ 305,000$$ .

note.source_type: Applied Example 7. The Rings of Neptune
note.title: Applied Example 7. The Rings of Neptune
note.heading: Applied Example 7. The Rings of Neptune

list.item: A ring has an inner radius of $$r$$ units and an outer radius of $$R$$ units, where $$(R - r)$$ is small in comparison to $$r$$ (Figure 23a). Use differentials to estimate the area of the ring. Figure 23 Details Two images a and b. Image a is an illustration showing a ring composed of two concentric circles. The radius of the inner circle is indicated by an arrow from the center to the circumference and is labeled r. The radius of the outer circle is indicated by an arrow from the center to the circumference and is labeled R. The thickness of the ring is labeled dr = R – r. Image b is a picture of the planet Neptune and its rings. Neptune is depicted as a blue sphere with two concentric rings. Courtesy of NASA

Recent observations, including those of Voyager I and II, showed that Neptune’s ring system is considerably more complex than had been believed. For one thing, it is made up of a large number of distinguishable rings rather than one continuous great ring as was previously thought (Figure 23b). The outermost ring, 1989N1R, has an inner radius of approximately $$62,900$$ kilometers (measured from the center of the planet) and a radial width of approximately $$50$$ kilometers. Using these data, estimate the area of the ring.

note.heading: Solution

list.item: Since the area of a circle of radius $$x$$ is $$A = f(x) = \pi x^{2}$$ , we find $$\begin{array}{l} {\pi R^{2} - \pi r^{2} = f(R) - f(r)} \\ {\phantom{\pi R^{2} - \pi r^{2}} = \Delta A \begin{array}{l} { \text{Remember,} \Delta A = \text{change in} f \text{when} x} \\ { \text{changes from} x = r \text{to} x = R.} \end{array}} \\ {\phantom{\pi R^{2} - \pi r^{2}} \approx dA} \\ {\phantom{\pi R^{2} - \pi r^{2}} = f^{\prime}(r)dr} \end{array}$$ where $$dr = R - r$$ . So we see that the area of the ring is approximately $$2\pi r(R - r)$$ square units. In words, the area of the ring is approximately equal to $${Circumference of the inner circle} \times {Thickness of the ring}$$

Applying the results of part (a) with $$r = 62,900$$ and $$dr = 50$$ , we find that the area of the ring is approximately $$2\pi(62,900)(50)$$ , or $$19,760,000$$ square kilometers, which is roughly $$4\%$$ of the earth’s surface.

section.paragraph: Before looking at the next example, we need to familiarize ourselves with some terminology. If a quantity with exact value $$q$$ is measured or calculated with an error of $$\Delta q$$ , then the quantity $$\Delta q \slash q$$ is called the relative error in the measurement or calculation of $$q$$ . If the quantity $$\Delta q \slash q$$ is expressed as a percentage, it is then called the percentage error. Because $$\Delta q$$ is approximated by $$dq$$ , we normally approximate the relative error $$\Delta q \slash q$$ by $$dq \slash q$$ .

note.source_type: Applied Example 8. Estimating Errors in Measurement
note.title: Applied Example 8. Estimating Errors in Measurement
note.heading: Applied Example 8. Estimating Errors in Measurement
note.paragraph: Suppose the radius of a ball bearing is measured to be $$0.5$$ inch, with a maximum error of $$\pm 0.0002$$ inch. Then, the relative error in $$r$$ is
$$\frac{dr}{r} = \frac{\pm 0.0002}{0.5} = \pm 0.0004 \text{Relative error}$$
and the percentage error is $$\pm 0.04\%$$ .
